theme: My companion stretched out his hand against me
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 55:1-23. David’s closest friend betrays him, and he longs to fly away. Notice the turn in verse 22, and read it against the betrayal in Luke 22.
settingTheScene: Psalm 55 is a psalm of David, probably from the time of Absalom’s rebellion, when his trusted advisor Ahithophel joined the conspiracy. David is in anguish. The city is full of violence, and the one who hurt him the most was a friend. It is one of the most honest psalms about betrayal, and it ends with one of the most quoted verses in the Psalter.
observation: “Give ear to my prayer, O God, and hide not yourself from my plea for mercy!” (v. 1).
“My heart is in anguish within me; the terrors of death have fallen upon me” (v. 4).
“Oh, that I had wings like a dove! I would fly away and be at rest” (v. 6).
“But it is you, a man, my equal, my companion, my familiar friend” (v. 13).
“We used to take sweet counsel together; within God’s house we walked in the throng” (v. 14).
“His speech was smooth as butter, yet war was in his heart” (v. 21).
“Cast your burden on the LORD, and he will sustain you; he will never permit the righteous to be moved” (v. 22).
interpretation:
David begins with a plea: “Give ear to my prayer.” He is restless, he moans, his heart is in anguish. Fear and trembling overwhelm him, and horror covers him. In the middle of that, he wishes he could escape: “Oh, that I had wings like a dove! I would fly away and be at rest.” Everyone has felt this. We want to flee the pain, find a quiet place, and wait out the storm.

The city is full of violence and strife, and iniquity and trouble are within it. But what hurts most is not the enemy outside. “It is not an enemy who taunts me; then I could bear it… But it is you, a man, my equal, my companion, my familiar friend.” They had walked together to the house of God. The betrayer had broken covenant. His speech was smooth as butter, “yet war was in his heart.”

Notice what David does. He does not hide his rage. He asks God to confuse the tongues of the wicked and to bring them down. But he also does something more: he calls on God, evening, morning, and noon, and God hears.

And then, the center of the psalm: “Cast your burden on the LORD, and he will sustain you; he will never permit the righteous to be moved.” David speaks to himself and to us. A burden you cannot carry can be put on someone who can. The word here is gift or lot, whatever has been given to you. Give it to the LORD, and he will hold you up. The final line is a short declaration: “But I will trust in you.”

Peter later quotes this verse: “Casting all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you.” And Jesus, betrayed in a garden by a friend with a kiss, lived this psalm. He cast his burden on the Father. In Gethsemane he prayed, “Not my will, but yours,” and he was sustained. His betrayal means that when we are betrayed, we have a High Priest who understands.
connection: 2 Samuel 15:12 and 17:23 tell of Ahithophel’s betrayal and death. Psalm 41:9 uses the same betrayal imagery. Matthew 26:47-50 shows Judas’s kiss. Luke 22:48 is Jesus’ word to Judas. 1 Peter 5:7 quotes verse 22. Philippians 4:6-7 invites us to bring everything to God in prayer. Hebrews 4:15 says Jesus can sympathize with our weaknesses. Matthew 11:28 invites the weary to come to him.
application:
Name your burden aloud and give it to the LORD. Do it again when it returns.

If you are tempted to run, ask where you can find rest, then go to him in prayer.

Pray for the one who hurt you. Entrust the justice to God.
prayerPrompts: Tell God the anguish of your heart.
Cast your burden on him and tell him what it is.
Thank him that he sustains you.
